meta.title: A mixed-method review of cash transfers and intimate partner violence in low- and middle-income countries
meta.topic: Cash transfers and intimate partner violence

brief.intended_change: Reduce intimate partner violence while avoiding unintended increases in violence associated with cash transfer programmes.
brief.population: Primarily women in poor and vulnerable households, including women in marital, cohabiting or dating relationships.
brief.place: Low- and middle-income countries; the reviewed evidence is concentrated in Latin America.
brief.time_horizon: Varies by programme and evaluation. The review includes data collected between 1998 and 2015; evidence on long-term effects and sustainability after transfers end is limited.
brief.intervention: Conditional and unconditional cash transfers, sometimes bundled with complementary services or in-kind transfers. Most reviewed programmes paid women monthly; reported transfer values ranged from approximately 6–50% of baseline household expenditure.
brief.context: Cash transfers are primarily poverty-alleviation and social protection programmes rather than violence-specific interventions. Their implications for violence may differ with programme design, household relationships and local gender norms.
brief.outcome_first: Develop a theory of change for reducing intimate partner violence among women in poor and vulnerable households in low- and middle-income countries. Account for differences between settings and the possibility of unintended harm.
brief.intervention_first: Develop a theory of change for conditional and unconditional cash transfer programmes serving poor and vulnerable households in low- and middle-income countries. Explain how these programmes could reduce intimate partner violence against women, and where unintended increases might occur.

key_claims.claim: Cash transfers can reduce intimate partner violence, although effects vary by violence measure, programme and population.
key_claims.where: Abstract; Table 2; Table 3; discussion, document pages 31–35

verdict.raw: Fourteen quantitative and nine qualitative studies met our inclusion criteria, of which eleven and six respectively demonstrated evidence that CTs decrease IPV. We found little support for increases in IPV, with only two studies showing overall mixed or adverse impacts. Transfers appear to reduce physical and/or sexual IPV more consistently than emotional abuse or controlling behaviours.
verdict.quote: eleven and six respectively demonstrated evidence that CTs decrease IPV

key_claims.claim: Cash transfers improve household economic security and reduce poverty, with possible economic spillovers to non-beneficiaries.

verdict.raw: There is a large and robust literature across different geographical regions and program typologies showing that in general, CTs have significant positive impacts on a range of household-level economic security outcomes. Further, there is a growing literature documenting the positive local economy impacts of CTs, implying positive spill-overs on non-beneficiary households in terms of economic outcomes.
verdict.quote: a large and robust literature

key_claims.claim: Greater economic security can reduce poverty-related stress and improve emotional wellbeing.
key_claims.where: Section 4.1, document pages 23–24; mechanisms summary, document page 15

verdict.raw: Overall, evidence confirms a strong relationship between poverty and mental health in developing settings. Although the relationship between poverty and poor mental health is well established, we know less about the typologies of interventions which are successful at breaking the two-way cycle. A recent review of programming concluded that although there is good evidence that a variety of mental health programs have positive impacts on economic outcomes, overall the mental health effects of poverty alleviation programs are inconclusive.
verdict.quote: the mental health effects of poverty alleviation programs are inconclusive

key_claims.claim: Improved emotional wellbeing reduces IPV directly or through reduced alcohol use as a negative coping mechanism.
key_claims.where: Section 4.1; Figure 1; qualitative mechanisms summary, document page 20; discussion, document page 31

verdict.raw: We found evidence to support all three hypothesized pathways: economic security and emotional wellbeing; intra-household conflict; and women’s empowerment. We also found substantial evidence from related literature to support each step in the proposed causal chains, with the exception of increasing violence by exacerbating conflict over the consumption of temptation goods.
verdict.quote: evidence to support all three hypothesized pathways

key_claims.claim: Cash available for daily household needs reduces tensions and relationship conflict, thereby reducing IPV.
key_claims.where: Table 3; qualitative mechanisms summary, document page 20; Figure 1; discussion, document page 31

verdict.raw: Reduction in household tensions leading to fewer conflicts (mentioned by 4 studies; Slater & Mphale, 2008, Yildrim 2011, Angeles 2012, Buller et al. 2016)
verdict.quote: Reduction in household tensions leading to fewer conflicts

key_claims.claim: Additional cash could increase purchases of temptation goods and provoke conflict and IPV, but this proposed adverse pathway lacks support.

verdict.raw: We also found substantial evidence from related literature to support each step in the proposed causal chains, with the exception of increasing violence by exacerbating conflict over the consumption of temptation goods.
verdict.quote: with the exception of increasing violence by exacerbating conflict over the consumption of temptation goods

key_claims.claim: Transfers to women can increase their financial autonomy, confidence and bargaining power, but empowerment effects are mixed and context-specific.
key_claims.where: Table 2; Table 3; mechanisms summaries, document pages 15 and 20; empowerment discussion, document page 29

verdict.raw: Numerous studies have also shown that CTs increase women’s savings and income earning opportunities, suggesting that CTs may affect women's bargaining power. However, the broader evidence is mixed. Although qualitative evidence on CCTs, largely from Latin America and the Caribbean, generally points to positive impacts on empowerment indicators, quantitative results are mixed.
verdict.quote: the broader evidence is mixed

key_claims.claim: Stronger bargaining power may reduce IPV when partners accept it, but threatened authority or attempts to extract transfers can produce backlash.
key_claims.where: Mechanisms summaries, document pages 15 and 20; Table 2; Table 3; Figure 1; discussion, document pages 31–32

verdict.raw: The economic security and emotional wellbeing pathway is the only one that exclusively reduces IPV; the other two may increase or decrease IPV, depending on whether additional cash aggravates or soothes relationship conflict and/or how men respond to women’s increased empowerment. A partner seeking to extract resources/CT from his wife was mentioned by Bobonis et al. 2013, however not tested directly. Male backlash was mentioned by Angelucci 2008, with evidence suggesting the pathway could be valid.
verdict.quote: the other two may increase or decrease IPV

key_claims.claim: Programme framing and the size and regularity of transfers can affect acceptance of changed household roles and the risk of IPV.

verdict.raw: Programs that generate smaller shifts in relationship power appear more easily accepted by men than those catalysing larger disruptions. More “acceptable” shifts might also be achieved by making smaller, more regular transfers. It should be noted, however, that the Kenya GiveDirectly study tested lump sum versus periodic transfers and found that the difference did not significantly affect the magnitude or impacts on IPV.
verdict.quote: the difference did not significantly affect the magnitude or impacts on IPV

key_claims.claim: Whether women or men receive the transfer may affect IPV pathways, but evidence comparing recipient sex is insufficient.
key_claims.where: Table 2, Kenya study; discussion, document page 32

verdict.raw: While empirical evidence is scarce and mixed in terms of the impact of recipient sex on economic and human capital outcomes of transfers, there is even less evidence for how different targeting schemes affect IPV outcomes. Across the studies reviewed here, the majority transferred cash to women; therefore, a large gap in knowledge remains with respect to impacts on IPV when men are the main recipient. Heterogeneous analysis by lump sum vs. monthly transfer, by large vs. small transfer & by male vs. female recipient in main sample show no differential impacts, however in the sample including within-cluster spillover HHs, impacts are driven by sample with large, monthly CTs given to females.
verdict.quote: a large gap in knowledge remains

key_claims.claim: Complementary services and programme participation may strengthen violence reductions through health, social ties and empowerment, but these mechanisms are not well isolated.
key_claims.where: Table 2, Bangladesh and Peru studies; Table 3, Ecuador study; mechanisms summary, document page 15; research gaps, document page 35

verdict.raw: Increasing interaction with the health sector, thereby improving women’s overall health and making her more resilient to abuse was mentioned by Ritter Burga 2014, including evidence suggesting the pathway could be valid. Encouraging greater interaction with other women and village leaders, which increases a woman’s social capital and social ties, and could increase the social cost of men perpetrating violence was mentioned by Roy et al. 2017, however not tested directly. Cross-sectional analysis on post-endline suggests transfers+BCC lead to sustainable reductions in IPV; transfers alone showed no significant post-endline impacts in the reported indicators. None were able to test potential synergistic effects between program components.
verdict.quote: none were able to test potential synergistic effects between program components

key_claims.claim: Violence reductions may change over time or after transfers stop, so short-term reductions do not establish sustained effects.
key_claims.where: Programme review, document page 13; research gaps and conclusion, document page 35

verdict.raw: Finally, we know little about long-term impacts, including how impacts may vary over time horizons and if impacts are non-linear, as well as the sustainability of impacts after CTs end or households graduate (the latter studied only by Roy et al. 2017).
verdict.quote: we know little about long-term impacts

overall.raw: We found evidence to support all three hypothesized pathways: economic security and emotional wellbeing; intra-household conflict; and women’s empowerment. We also found substantial evidence from related literature to support each step in the proposed causal chains, with the exception of increasing violence by exacerbating conflict over the consumption of temptation goods.
overall.quote: We found evidence to support all three hypothesized pathways

conclusions.summary: Cash transfers are promising tools for reducing IPV, with little support for overall increases. The review supports three pathways, but only economic security and emotional wellbeing exclusively predicts reductions; conflict and empowerment may increase or decrease violence depending on relationship dynamics and context. The temptation-goods conflict pathway is the exception to the generally supportive related evidence. Physical and sexual violence show more consistent reductions than emotional abuse or controlling behaviours. Direct measurement of mechanisms, programme design comparisons, regional coverage and evidence on long-term sustainability remain limited.
recommendations: Use internationally validated IPV measures sensitive to programme effects, including frequency and severity.
Go beyond impact estimation to measure causal pathways credibly, particularly relationship dynamics and intra-household behaviour.
Test targeting, complementary programming, programme linkages and conditionalities, including possible synergies between components.
Examine programme framing and design features that can maximize benefits and mitigate adverse impacts.
Fill regional and contextual gaps, including Asia, the Middle East, Western and Central Africa, and humanitarian settings.
Study long-term effects and sustainability after transfers end or households graduate.

The broad coloured proximate-outcome and pathway panels are treated as containers because yellow arrows connect their boundaries as units. Those arrows meet the pathway-title bands rather than individual result boxes; the titles have not been made into boxes.
The four proximate-outcome circles are joined by thick yellow connectors without visible arrowheads. No causal links between those circles have been added.
No separate arrow from the programme-design polygon to the proximate-outcome panel is clearly visible. The polygon itself is arrow-shaped; no additional link has been inferred.
“INCREASED” is a shared modifier above the four proximate outcomes, accompanied by a triangular graphic; it has not been transcribed as a separate result box.

Intermediate pathways have no explicit short-term versus long-term headings. Early pathway results are mapped to outcome_short and subsequent relationship or wellbeing results to outcome_long; this is a layer interpretation, not a timing claim made by the figure.
The supplied excerpts omit portions of the pathway evidence sections. The broad discussion verdict is retained on the relevant key claims, but is not automatically assigned to every individual arrow.

The conclusion identifies the temptation-goods chain as lacking supporting evidence, but does not isolate whether the evidential failure is cash-to-consumption, consumption-to-conflict, or conflict-to-IPV. Its verdict is placed on l_temptation_conflict and the full chain is covered by k_temptation.
Strongest links are those explicitly described as having a large and robust literature or a strong relationship; the source does not provide a formal ranking.
Organisation, document URLs and licence were not supplied. The year is taken from the case notes.
